answers.answer: Redis is an in-memory key-value store and data structure server: a network server mapping keys to typed values (strings, lists, sets, hashes, sorted sets, streams, etc.) kept primarily in RAM, with optional persistence to disk (RDB snapshots, AOF). It is meant for real-time applications where an on-disk database is too slow on the request path: caching (with eviction and expiration), session stores, queues and messaging (lists, sorted sets, pub/sub, streams), and search/vector similarity (vector sets in beta).

answers.answer: RDB snapshots are point-in-time dumps of the whole dataset taken by a forked child when configured save points are reached; a crash or power outage may lose a few minutes of writes. The AOF logs every write command and is replayed at startup; with appendfsync everysec it can lose about one second of writes, so it gives better durability. When both are enabled, Redis loads the AOF at startup because it has the better durability guarantees.

answers.answer: The event loop (library in ae.c, aeMain) sleeps until file descriptors are ready and then processes their events, repeating until stopped. The connection layer: the listening socket's handler connSocketAcceptHandler (socket.c) accepts TCP connections and passes them to acceptCommonHandler, which creates a client; createClient installs readQueryFromClient as the read handler. Per turn: ready sockets trigger readQueryFromClient, which fills the query buffer and calls processInputBuffer to parse and execute full commands; replies go into client output buffers; before sleeping again, beforeSleep flushes the AOF (flushAppendOnlyFile) and calls handleClientsWithPendingWrites to send buffered replies. serverCron runs periodic work such as checking save points. Further detail of a turn (e.g. timers ordering): not stated.

answers.answer: connSocketAcceptHandler accepts the connection and acceptCommonHandler creates a client; readQueryFromClient (read handler) fills the query buffer and calls processInputBuffer, which picks multibulk (starts with *) or inline protocol, parses arguments, and calls processCommandAndResetClient. processCommand looks up the command, checks ACL permissions, redirects keys owned by another cluster node, runs eviction when maxmemory is set (writes fail with noeviction when memory is full), and refuses writes after a persistence error. Inside MULTI the command is queued and answered QUEUED; otherwise call runs the command's proc. The reply goes into the output buffer via addReply. call hands the write to alsoPropagate; propagateNow feeds it to feedAppendOnlyFile (AOF buffer) and replicationFeedSlaves (replication stream). In beforeSleep, flushAppendOnlyFile writes the AOF buffer to disk before replies are sent, then handleClientsWithPendingWrites sends replies. fsync timing depends on appendfsync.

answers.answer: A replica connects with SYNC or PSYNC (handled by syncCommand). After a short disconnect it can resume partially from the master's replication backlog (a buffer of recent writes) instead of a full resync; otherwise a full resynchronization occurs. The exact decision criteria and what happens in each case in detail: not stated.

answers.answer: The manifesto prefers an efficient mostly single-threaded core because threading is not a silver bullet and a single-threaded core keeps the design simple; scaling is done by combining many shared-nothing single-threaded instances (e.g. Redis Cluster), which suits NUMA. Extra threads: optional I/O threads (io-threads) read, parse and write sockets off the main thread (disabled by default); background saves use a forked child process. Costs/conditions: maintainers suggest I/O threads only on machines with at least four cores and only for a real performance problem; threaded I/O is not supported for TLS connections; repl-compression works only with io-threads above 1. Single-threaded cost: one slow command delays all other clients of that instance.

answers.answer: appendfsync sets how often the AOF is fsynced; everysec (fsync once a second) is described as a compromise, losing about one second of writes; the other policies' trade-offs: not stated. The log is flushed in beforeSleep, before replies are sent, because the AOF must be written before replying to the client. Durability given up during a background save with the related mitigation enabled: not stated.

answers.answer: When maxmemory is reached, keys are evicted according to maxmemory-policy; with the default noeviction (or when no key can be evicted), write commands that need memory get errors. processCommand runs eviction when maxmemory is set. answers.answer: If a background save fails, Redis by default stops accepting writes so the failure is noticed (processCommand refuses writes after a persistence error). Behaviour with a damaged AOF at startup and when the data file cannot be loaded: not stated.

answers.answer: Replication is asynchronous, so acknowledged writes can be lost on failover; it does not guarantee that N replicas accept a write. An operator can configure the master to stop accepting writes if it is not connected to at least a given number of replicas, which limits the window of exposure for lost writes to a specified number of seconds. Sentinel can promote a replica (lowest priority number, never priority 0). How a replica behaves towards clients when its link to the master is down: not stated.
